questions.stem: What is the main purpose of criminal law?
options: To set out the powers of parliament and the way government must be organised
To settle disagreements between private parties over contracts and property
To protect society by defining and punishing conduct that harms the community
To let individuals recover compensation from people who have caused them a loss
questions.explanation: Criminal law treats certain conduct as a wrong against the whole community, so the state prosecutes and punishes offenders to protect society. Compensation for loss and contract disputes belong to civil law.

questions.stem: In a NSW criminal case, the case is brought in the name of the Crown (R v Smith). This shows that:
options: a crime is treated as a wrong against the whole community, not only the victim
the victim must pay for the prosecution and decides whether the case goes ahead
only the King personally can decide whether a person is guilty of an offence
criminal cases are private disputes between the accused and the person harmed
questions.explanation: Criminal proceedings are brought by the state, represented by the Crown, because crimes harm society as a whole. The victim is usually a witness rather than a party, and does not control the prosecution.

questions.stem: The actus reus of a crime is:
options: the physical act or omission that makes up the offence
the guilty state of mind of the accused at the time of the act
the link between the accused's conduct and the harm
the punishment set by parliament for the offence
questions.explanation: Actus reus, the 'guilty act', is the conduct element: the act, omission or state of affairs the offence prohibits, and it must be voluntary. The guilty state of mind is mens rea, and the link to the harm is causation.

questions.stem: Which list contains the forms of mens rea recognised in criminal law?
options: Intention, provocation and strict liability
Recklessness, deterrence and voluntariness
Intention, recklessness and criminal negligence
Voluntariness, causation and criminal negligence
questions.explanation: Mens rea can take the form of intention (meaning to cause the result), recklessness (foreseeing the risk and going ahead) or, for some offences, criminal negligence. Voluntariness belongs to the actus reus, and causation is a separate element.

questions.stem: Leo throws a rock at a car, knowing there is a real chance it could hit the driver, but hoping it will not. It hits and injures her. Leo's state of mind is best described as:
options: voluntariness
strict liability
recklessness
intention
questions.explanation: Leo foresaw the risk of harm and went ahead anyway, which is recklessness. Intention would require that he meant to hit her, and voluntariness describes whether the act itself was willed, not his attitude to the result.

questions.stem: Ava punches Ben, who falls and is taken to hospital. While there he suffers a minor complication from routine treatment and dies. The prosecution must prove causation. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Ava cannot be a cause because any medical treatment breaks the chain of causation
Ava is automatically a cause because she committed an assault on Ben first
Causation is not an element when the accused intended to cause some harm
Ava's act can still be a cause if it remained a substantial cause of death
questions.explanation: The prosecution must prove the accused's act was a substantial cause of the result; ordinary medical treatment does not usually break the chain of causation unless it is so extraordinary that it becomes the real cause. Committing an assault does not automatically prove causation of death.

questions.stem: Which situation shows that the actus reus must be voluntary?
options: A driver who chooses to speed and hits a pedestrian may lack a voluntary act
A driver who drinks heavily and then hits a pedestrian may lack a voluntary act
A driver who texts at the wheel and hits a pedestrian may lack a voluntary act
A driver who suffers a sudden seizure and hits a pedestrian may lack a voluntary act
questions.explanation: An act done during a sudden seizure is not willed by the accused, so the voluntariness required for the actus reus may be missing. Speeding, drinking and texting are all choices the driver made.

questions.stem: A strict liability offence is one where:
options: the accused must prove their own innocence in court
the offence can be tried only before a judge and jury
the prosecution does not need to prove mens rea
the prosecution does not need to prove actus reus
questions.explanation: For strict liability offences, such as many traffic offences, proving the prohibited act is enough; the prosecution need not prove intention or recklessness. The prosecution still carries the burden of proving the act.

questions.stem: A driver charged with a strict liability offence shows she honestly and reasonably believed in facts which, if true, would have made her conduct lawful. Which statement is correct?
options: This defence of honest and reasonable mistake of fact may be available for strict liability
This defence is never available, because strict liability means mens rea must be proved
This defence is available only for summary offences heard before a jury in the District Court
This defence works only if she can prove her mistake beyond reasonable doubt to the jury
questions.explanation: Strict liability offences remove the need to prove mens rea but generally still allow the defence of honest and reasonable mistake of fact. Absolute liability offences do not allow even that defence. Summary offences are heard by a magistrate, not a jury.

questions.stem: In NSW, summary offences are:
options: offences that can be proved without showing the accused had a guilty mind
offences committed by young people and heard only in the Children's Court
less serious offences heard and determined by a magistrate in the Local Court
serious offences heard before a judge and jury in the District or Supreme Court
questions.explanation: Summary offences, such as offensive language under the Summary Offences Act 1988 (NSW), are minor offences heard by a magistrate without a jury. Serious offences tried by judge and jury are indictable offences.

questions.stem: Under the Criminal Procedure Act 1986 (NSW), a Table 1 offence is an indictable offence that is:
options: always heard in the Children's Court, because it involves an offender under 18
dealt with summarily unless the prosecution or the accused elects a trial on indictment
dealt with summarily unless the prosecution alone elects to have the trial on indictment
always tried before a judge and jury, because neither party may make any election
questions.explanation: Table 1 and Table 2 offences are indictable offences dealt with summarily in the Local Court by default. For Table 1 offences either the prosecution or the accused may elect to go on indictment, while for Table 2 offences only the prosecution may elect.

questions.stem: Why does NSW allow many indictable offences to be dealt with summarily in the Local Court?
options: It is cheaper and faster, reducing delay while keeping serious cases in the higher courts
It guarantees the accused a jury trial while avoiding the cost of paying a District Court judge
It allows magistrates to impose longer sentences than judges in the higher courts
It removes the prosecution's duty to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt in minor cases
questions.explanation: Hearing less serious indictable offences summarily saves time and money for the courts and the parties, and leaves the District and Supreme Courts free for the most serious matters. Magistrates have lower sentencing limits, and the standard of proof is the same in every criminal court.

questions.stem: Which offence is best classified as a crime against property?
options: Breaking into a house and stealing a laptop
Assault occasioning actual bodily harm to a person
Manslaughter caused by a single punch
Threatening a person with a knife
questions.explanation: Break and enter with theft targets another person's property, so it is a crime against property. Assault, manslaughter and threatening with a weapon all harm or threaten a person, so they are crimes against the person.

questions.stem: Which statement about murder under the Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) is correct?
options: It is a strict liability offence, so the prosecution does not need to prove any mental element
It is a crime against property when it happens during a robbery or a break-in at a house
It is a crime against the person and an indictable offence with a maximum of life imprisonment
It is a summary offence because it involves only one victim and is heard in the Local Court
questions.explanation: Murder is the most serious crime against the person; it is strictly indictable and carries a maximum penalty of imprisonment for life. It requires proof of a mental element such as intent to kill or reckless indifference to human life, so it is not strict liability.

questions.stem: In a NSW criminal trial, who carries the burden of proof and to what standard?
options: The prosecution, beyond reasonable doubt
The accused, beyond reasonable doubt
The prosecution, on the balance of probabilities
The accused, on the balance of probabilities
questions.explanation: The prosecution must prove each element of the offence beyond reasonable doubt, which reflects the presumption of innocence. The balance of probabilities is the lower civil standard.

questions.stem: Why is the standard of proof in criminal cases set higher than in civil cases?
options: Criminal cases are heard only in superior courts, which use stricter rules than lower courts
A conviction can mean loss of liberty and a criminal record, so wrongful convictions must be avoided
Criminal trials always have juries, and juries cannot apply a standard as low as the civil one
The accused always has a lawyer funded by Legal Aid NSW, so the prosecution needs a harder test
questions.explanation: Because the consequences of conviction are so serious, the law accepts that some guilty people may be acquitted rather than risk convicting the innocent. Many criminal cases are heard by magistrates without juries, and the same standard applies in every criminal court.

questions.stem: How do NSW police most commonly start criminal proceedings against a person?
options: By asking a jury to decide whether there is enough evidence to lay a charge
By writing to the High Court to request permission to begin a prosecution
By issuing a court attendance notice that sets out the charge and when to attend court
By filing a statement of claim in the Local Court that sets out the damages sought
questions.explanation: Criminal proceedings in NSW are usually started with a court attendance notice, which tells the accused the offence charged and the date of their first court appearance. A statement of claim starts civil proceedings.

questions.stem: After a person is charged with a strictly indictable offence in NSW, a senior prosecutor files a document confirming the charges that will proceed. This document is a:
options: committal warrant
charge certificate
case conference
statement of claim
questions.explanation: Under the 2018 early appropriate guilty plea reforms, the prosecution files a charge certificate confirming the charges to be prosecuted. A case conference is the meeting between prosecution and defence that follows, to discuss whether the accused will plead guilty.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the mandatory case conference held in NSW before an indictable matter is committed to a higher court?
options: To let the magistrate decide whether the accused is guilty before any trial takes place
To select the jury that will hear the trial and to decide which jurors can be excused
To allow the victim to question the accused directly about the offence before trial
To encourage early resolution, such as an appropriate guilty plea, before a trial is listed
questions.explanation: The case conference brings the prosecution and the defence lawyer together to narrow the issues and consider whether an appropriate guilty plea can be agreed, which reduces delay and saves trial costs. Guilt is not decided at committal, and juries are chosen only when a trial starts.

questions.stem: In committal proceedings in the Local Court for an indictable offence, the magistrate:
options: sends the case to a higher court for trial or for sentence
decides the accused's guilt and then imposes a sentence
selects twelve jurors to hear the trial in the Local Court
hears the accused's appeal against an earlier conviction
questions.explanation: Committal is the process by which a strictly indictable matter is moved from the Local Court to the District or Supreme Court, for trial if the accused pleads not guilty or for sentence if they plead guilty. Juries do not sit in the Local Court.

questions.stem: Which organisation provides free or low-cost legal representation to eligible people in NSW criminal cases?
options: Legal Aid NSW
The NSW Ombudsman
The Office of the Sheriff
The Legislation Review Committee
questions.explanation: Legal Aid NSW provides legal advice and representation to people who meet its means and merit tests. The Sheriff's Office runs jury service and court security, and the Ombudsman investigates complaints about government agencies.

questions.stem: In Dietrich v The Queen (1992), the High Court held that:
options: every accused person in Australia has an absolute right to a lawyer paid for by the state in all criminal cases
an accused who represents themselves in a serious trial must be convicted if the evidence against them is strong
legal aid bodies must fund a lawyer for any accused who asks, whatever their income and the nature of the charge
a trial for a serious offence may be stayed if an accused who cannot afford a lawyer is unrepresented through no fault of their own
questions.explanation: Dietrich established that there is no absolute right to state-funded counsel, but that a trial for a serious offence may be adjourned or stayed if an indigent accused is unrepresented through no fault of their own, because the trial would be unfair. It is a key case on the right to a fair trial.

questions.stem: Why does legal representation matter to achieving justice in a criminal trial?
options: Juries must convict any accused who chooses to represent themselves at the trial
The adversarial system relies on each side presenting and testing evidence effectively
Judges will not allow an accused to plead not guilty unless a lawyer is present in court
Only a lawyer can ask for the standard of proof to be lowered in the accused's favour
questions.explanation: In an adversarial trial the judge stays neutral, so an unrepresented accused may struggle with procedure, rules of evidence and cross-examination. An accused may represent themselves and may plead not guilty without a lawyer.

questions.stem: Who prosecutes most serious indictable offences in the NSW District and Supreme Courts?
options: The Sheriff of NSW and court officers
The Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions
Police prosecutors from the NSW Police Force
Legal Aid NSW on behalf of the victim
questions.explanation: The Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP) prosecutes serious indictable matters in the higher courts, independently of government. Police prosecutors conduct most prosecutions in the Local Court, and Legal Aid NSW mainly defends accused people.

questions.stem: What is the main role of a defence barrister in a criminal trial?
options: To decide which evidence the jury is allowed to hear and to direct it on the law
To prove to the jury beyond reasonable doubt that the accused is innocent of every charge laid
To manage the jury, keep order in the courtroom and enforce the court's orders
To present the accused's case and test the prosecution evidence through cross-examination
questions.explanation: Defence barristers argue the accused's case and challenge the prosecution's evidence, but they do not have to prove innocence. Ruling on evidence and directing the jury is the judge's role, and the Sheriff's officers keep order and manage juries.

questions.stem: In a NSW criminal jury trial, the role of the judge is to:
options: investigate the offence and call witnesses who were not chosen by either party
represent the community's interests by arguing for a conviction against the accused
decide questions of law, direct the jury and pass sentence if there is a conviction
decide whether the accused is guilty after hearing all of the evidence in the case
questions.explanation: In a jury trial the judge rules on law and evidence, instructs the jury and sentences the offender if convicted, while the jury decides the facts and the verdict. Arguing for conviction is the prosecutor's role.

questions.stem: How many jurors sit on a NSW criminal trial jury?
questions.explanation: Under the Jury Act 1977 (NSW), a criminal trial jury is made up of 12 people chosen at random from the electoral roll. Civil juries in NSW usually have 4 jurors.

questions.stem: In a NSW trial for a state offence, a jury of 12 cannot agree. In what circumstances may the judge accept an 11 to 1 majority verdict?
options: Only if the accused has pleaded guilty to a lesser charge and the jury is deciding on the more serious one
After at least eight hours of deliberation, if satisfied by examining a juror on oath that unanimity is unlikely
After at least two hours of deliberation, if the prosecution and the defence both ask the judge to accept it
At any time during deliberation, if the jury foreperson tells the judge that only one juror disagrees
questions.explanation: Section 55F of the Jury Act 1977 (NSW) allows a majority verdict only after the jury has deliberated for a reasonable time of at least eight hours and the court is satisfied, after examining one or more jurors on oath, that a unanimous verdict is unlikely. Both conditions must be strictly met.

questions.stem: A jury in a NSW court is trying a person charged on indictment with a Commonwealth offence. Can it return a majority verdict?
options: No, because Commonwealth offences can never be tried by a jury in any state court
No, because the High Court has held that federal jury trials require a unanimous verdict
Yes, because majority verdicts are allowed for every offence once eight hours have passed
Yes, because Commonwealth offences are always tried under the Jury Act 1977 (NSW) rules
questions.explanation: In Cheatle v The Queen (1993), the High Court held that the trial by jury guarantee in section 80 of the Constitution requires a unanimous verdict for Commonwealth offences tried on indictment. NSW majority verdicts are therefore available only for state offences.

questions.stem: Which statement about the strengths of the jury system is most accurate?
options: It allows jurors to research the case online so they can understand the evidence fully
It brings community standards into the verdict and spreads the decision across ordinary citizens
It produces faster verdicts than a judge alone because twelve people share the workload
It ensures that jurors give written reasons, so verdicts can be checked for legal errors
questions.explanation: Juries let members of the community decide guilt, which supports public confidence and reflects community values. Juries do not give reasons, they often take longer than judges, and jurors are forbidden from researching the case.

questions.stem: Under section 3A of the Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999 (NSW), which is a purpose of sentencing?
options: To give the victim's family control of the sentence
To raise money to fund the state's court system
To promote the rehabilitation of the offender
To compensate the offender for time spent in custody
questions.explanation: Section 3A lists seven purposes: adequate punishment, deterrence, protecting the community, rehabilitation, making the offender accountable, denouncing the conduct, and recognising the harm done to the victim and the community. Victims may make an impact statement but do not decide sentences.

questions.stem: A judge imposes a long sentence and states that it should discourage others in the community from committing similar crimes. This aim is:
options: general deterrence
specific deterrence
rehabilitation
incapacitation
questions.explanation: General deterrence aims to discourage the wider community from offending by showing the consequences. Specific deterrence targets the offender, and incapacitation protects the community by removing the offender's ability to reoffend, for example through imprisonment.

questions.stem: Which NSW sentencing option is a term of imprisonment served in the community under strict conditions, rather than in jail?
options: A community correction order with supervision
A penalty notice
An intensive correction order
A conditional release order
questions.explanation: An intensive correction order can only be made after the court decides a prison sentence is appropriate; the offender serves it in the community under supervision and conditions. Community correction orders and conditional release orders are non-custodial orders, and a penalty notice is an on-the-spot fine.

questions.stem: A first-time offender commits a minor offence and shows genuine remorse. The magistrate wants to give a chance to stay out of trouble, possibly without recording a conviction. The most suitable order is a:
options: conditional release order
intensive correction order
sentence of full-time imprisonment
suspended sentence of imprisonment
questions.explanation: A conditional release order requires the offender to be of good behaviour and can be made with or without a conviction, which suits a minor first offence. An intensive correction order is a form of imprisonment, and suspended sentences were abolished in NSW in 2018.

questions.stem: Why might a court impose a fine rather than imprisonment for a minor offence?
options: It has the same effect on every offender regardless of their income or wealth
It protects the community by removing the offender's ability to commit offences
It punishes the offender without the high cost and harmful effects of imprisonment
It guarantees that the offender will be rehabilitated and will never reoffend again
questions.explanation: Fines are cheap to administer and avoid the disruption and negative influences of prison, so they suit minor offences. However, a fine has a heavier impact on poorer offenders, and it does not incapacitate anyone.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates how the criminal justice system balances the rights of the accused with the interests of society?
options: Society's interests always outweigh the rights of the accused, so the burden of proof falls on the defence
The rights of the accused and of society never conflict, because both depend only on the facts of the case
Protections like the presumption of innocence guard against wrongful convictions, though some guilty people may go free
The rights of the accused always outweigh society's interests, so convictions are almost impossible to obtain
questions.explanation: Rights such as the presumption of innocence and the high standard of proof protect individuals from the power of the state, accepting that some guilty people will be acquitted. The burden of proof stays on the prosecution, and many people accused of crimes are convicted.

questions.stem: A court provides an interpreter at no cost for an accused who speaks little English. Which concept of justice does this most directly support?
options: Retribution, because the punishment will match the seriousness of the crime
Fairness, because the accused can understand and take part in the trial
Deterrence, because other people will be discouraged from offending
Precedent, because the case can then be followed in later decisions
questions.explanation: An accused who cannot understand the proceedings cannot respond to the case against them, so providing an interpreter supports a fair trial and, more broadly, access to the system. Deterrence and retribution are aims of punishment, not concepts of procedural justice.
